A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same sPHNN research, with matching architecture, stability theorem and four application domains. The main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions to be distinguished from relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training and prediction results for a spinning rigid body, cascaded tanks, thermal food processing and additive manufacturing, including extrapolation and augmented-state experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds baseline comparisons, training-data and noise studies, equilibrium-estimation results and computational timings.

M1.justification: The proposed sPHNN retains its normalized convex Hamiltonian, constrained matrices and derivative/trajectory fitting procedures. Learning the equilibrium location was already supported and tested in v1. The POD description in v2 expands the existing truncated-SVD procedure. bPHNN is introduced as a comparison model.

E1.justification: All four application domains remain. v2 adds a food-processing scenario with Gaussian-corrupted input and temperature observations during training, followed by evaluation on clean data (Section 4.3, Table 1). Additional food-processing trajectories otherwise remain within the existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v1 primarily compares sPHNN with NODE and PHNN, adding sPHNN-LM for tanks. v2 evaluates bounded PHNNs across the applications, adds Kolter–Manek sNODEs to the rigid-body comparison, and extends sPHNN-LM to the other applications. The bPHNN comparator is an OnsagerNet-inspired adaptation supporting time-dependent inputs, not an evaluation of unchanged OnsagerNet.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled food-processing experiments varying training-set size from one to fifteen trajectories, plus 5%, 15% and 25% Gaussian-noise conditions with evaluation on clean training and test data. These substantially expand the evaluation design. Existing training budgets, learning rates, network widths and core benchmark settings remain; v1 already specifies the fifteen-trajectory food test set despite its erroneous Figure 6 caption.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of data requirements and noise robustness, expands fixed-versus-learned equilibrium comparisons, and tests the weaker boundedness constraint through bPHNN. Existing augmented-dimension and tank extrapolation studies remain, with saturation moved to Appendix D. Conversely, the direct comparison between learned Hamiltonians and physical energy in v1 Figure 3 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten rigid-body model instances and twenty instances per configuration for the other benchmarks, using boxplots and interquartile means/ranges to summarize variability. Added comparisons retain these practices. No increased repeat counts, seed specifications, confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive comparator, data-size, noise and timing results. For example, Table 1 reports sPHNN test RMSEs of 1.170, 2.595 and 3.177 at increasing noise levels, versus bPHNN's 1.572, 2.828 and 5.231. Section 4.1 newly reports an equilibrium-estimation distance of 0.010 for sPHNN-LM. The learned-Hamiltonian curves and energy-recovery finding from v1 Figure 3 are dropped.

T1.justification: The central stability theorem and proof remain. Appendix A adds a Hessian condition to Lemma A.1 and an alternative coercivity argument; the main text removes v1's asserted finite-time zero-dissipation condition for nonconverging solutions. These are limited mathematical revisions. The new assertion that strict convexity requires an everywhere positive-definite Hessian is incorrect.

C1.justification: The central claims about physically structured, globally stable learning from sparse data and surrogate modeling remain. v2's introduction and conclusion add the claim that providing the equilibrium as prior knowledge improves accuracy and reduces data requirements. Its novelty claim is also refined through more specific comparisons with existing stable models.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation of the equilibrium prior, explaining its advantage under scarce data and distinguishing bounded trajectories from convergence to the appropriate equilibrium. It adds a low-pass-filter explanation for noise robustness and discusses sNODE trajectory-training failures. It also clarifies that convexity is sufficient rather than necessary, discusses input warping, and reframes applicability around globally stable behavior within the region of interest.

D1.justification: v2 newly provides a stated code/model-weight access link, Glorot initialization, hardware and operating-system details, computational timings, additional training-trajectory identifiers and explicit latent encoder/decoder formulas. These materially improve reproducibility documentation. Some detail is lost when matrix parameterization is condensed, including explicit output dimensions and the softplus/absolute-value rules for Cholesky diagonals.

R1.justification: v2 replaces v1's broad statement that the intersection of physical structure and stability is largely unexplored with substantive comparisons to latent linear port-Hamiltonian identification, OnsagerNet and projection-based stable learning. Discussions of Rettberg, Yu and Schlaginhaufen distinguish nonlinear global stability, time-dependent inputs and trajectory-training compatibility. This changes the research positioning beyond routine citation updates.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: port-Hamiltonian motivation and rigid-body equations move into the background, the random-model experiment becomes part of the architecture explanation, matrix descriptions are consolidated, and tank setup/saturation material moves to a new appendix. The introduction, experimental discussion and conclusion are extensively revised.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with substantial figure redesign. Architecture and random dynamics are combined; comparison plots are split into panels; food-processing plots are expanded; manufacturing figures gain heat-source and comparator displays. New noise/timing tables and a latent-model diagram appear. The manufacturing error plot and tank saturation plots are relocated and expanded.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central contribution. v1's comparisons largely establish advantages over models without stability guarantees; v2 adds bounded and stable comparators and controlled studies separating equilibrium knowledge, data availability and noise robustness. These address important weaknesses in attributing the reported benefits. Better research positioning and new reproducibility information further improve assessability. The gains outweigh the removed energy-recovery diagnostic and localized problems, including Table 1's median/average wording inconsistency and Appendix A's incorrect strict-convexity remark; the central architecture and stability proof are retained.
